source: Newton's Third Law Pairs
The two forces of a pair act on different objects, are the same type and are equal in size.
Students call weight and the normal force a third-law pair, or think the heavier object pushes harder.
Newton's Third Law said forces come in pairs. With Free-Body Diagrams we can say exactly which forces pair up, and it is not always the pair you expect.

If A exerts a force on B, then B exerts a force on A that is equal in size, opposite in direction and of the same type. The two forces act on different objects, so they never appear on the same free-body diagram.

A force is an interaction between two objects, and an interaction has two ends. When your hand pushes a wall, the wall pushes your hand: one interaction, seen from each side. Because the forces act on different objects, they can't cancel each other; each changes the motion of its own object according to that object's mass.
A hand pushes block A, which pushes block B. The contact forces between A and B are a third-law pair: same size, opposite directions, on different blocks.
Worked examples
Earth pulls a book down with gravity. What is the third-law partner of that force?
Finding the partner
The book's gravitational pull on Earth, upward
Swap the objects: the book pulls Earth.
Same type (gravity), same size, opposite direction: the book pulls Earth up.
The table's upward push on the book is not the partner: it acts on the same object (the book) and is a different type (a contact force).
A $2{,}000\ \text{kg}$ truck bumps a $1{,}000\ \text{kg}$ car, pushing it with $8{,}000\ \text{N}$. Find each one's acceleration.
Unequal masses
Car $8\ \text{m/s}^2$; truck $4\ \text{m/s}^2$
Third law: the car pushes the truck with $8{,}000\ \text{N}$ too.
Equal forces, unequal effects: the lighter car gets the bigger acceleration.

Calling weight and the normal force a third-law pair (they act on the same object, and they aren't always equal, as in an elevator), or thinking the heavier or faster object pushes harder.
